name: Valley of Bri Leith
summary: The valley of the fairy mound east of Lough Derg: Caille, Brynach and the fort of Druim Cain, the empyreans of the high ground, the faerie horses and the Old Hermit's tent.

facts.text: In Irish myth Brí Léith is the sídh (fairy mound) of Midir, who loved Étaín and won her back from the king of Tara in the Tochmarc Étaíne.
Cad Goddeu ('the Battle of the Trees') is a medieval Welsh poem in the Book of Taliesin in which Gwydion brings the trees to life to fight.

Zone 206 (region 200, x 385,024-450,560, y 483,328-548,864): 363 monsters. Towns: Caille (area at 420,684/516,178; Ainrebh the enchanter, Lysagh, Ariana, Brynn), Brynach (409,987/528,096) and Druim Cain (421,166/484,998, radius 3,500: a fort of Master Rangers, Master Eldritch, Champions and Keep Sentinels, a siege merchant, trainers of every path and Channeler Ynsalg, the Druim Ligen Emissary). The Coruscating Mine entrance is at 397,971/488,565.

facts.text: Living Server lore: the valley as Midir's mound country; the empyreans as the mound's old servants; the siog; the faerie horses; the hermit and the dark druids who came over from southern Albion after the tree-song; Druim Cain as the eastern door; Moon Lake; the Old Hermit's book.

story:
The old songs say Bri Leith was Midir's: the mound of a lord of the Sidhe who loved a woman of the mortal kings and won her back from Tara by a game of chess and a pair of swans. The valley that bears the mound's name lies east of Lough Derg, low in the middle, with Caille and Brynach in its floor and high ground all round, and the people of Caille say the mound is still there, under the empyreans' heights in the east, and that its lord has not come out of it since the Veil came down.

The empyreans keep the heights. They are bright things, guardians and overseers and watchers, elders and wisps and orbs that drift down toward the lake country, and the druids of the realm think they were the mound's servants, set to keep its doors when its lord went in, and that they have gone on keeping them ever since with no lord to report to. They do not like the realm on their heights. Guardian Hru and Niy the Overseer keep the highest ground, and Keeper Rasa and Watcher Rylie hold the slopes below, and the empyrean keepers of the north-east carry swords that the chief of Culraid wants for his own reasons.

The valley floor is the fair folk's country in the plainer sense. Faerie horses and steeds graze the meadow by the guard post southwest of Caille, and faerie drakes nest above it, and the veil wisps that drift through the grass at dusk are, the Caille folk say, threads come loose from the Veil itself. The siog, the siabra of the valley, keep camps on the western hills, seekers and footpads and waylayers, and rob the road to the Silvermine. South-east of Caille, across Moon Lake, the mad changelings live at the foot of the hills behind the tall standing stones, the ones who were swapped in cradles and never swapped back, and their leader Lusmorebane is the maddest of them.

In the north of the valley, beside the faerie horse meadow, an old man keeps a tent. The realm calls him only the Old Hermit. He is a druid of the oldest craft, the craft of the trees, and he sleeps a great deal and wakes at odd seasons, and when he wakes the realm's young are sent to him from four directions with the things he needs: a druid's plant and a key, a jewel taken from a child of the Azure, a scroll from a druid the cliff siabra held, the head of a dark druid. The dark druid is Riocard, who keeps a high place in the west of the valley with five druids who came over from southern Albion. The Caille folk say they came for the hermit's craft, the old song that makes trees stand up and fight, which the bards of Albion have their own poem about. The hermit says nothing. Mikka the map-reader camps beside him and reads the half of an enchanted map that leads, Howth says, to Nuada's silver.

Caille is the valley's town, a low place of merchants and an enchanter, Ainrebh, who studies the crystal that ate a man in the Bog of Cullen and sends the realm to the Druid Prince with it. Fury sprites came into Caille once and mugged the armourer Lysagh for a green crystal, and the town has not let him forget it. Brynach is the smaller stop to the north. Druim Cain is the fort at the valley's south end, garrisoned like Druim Ligen, with master rangers and master eldritch on its walls and the Druim Ligen emissary's fire inside: the eastern door to the frontier. In the hills to the west the dark court cut its own door into the Coruscating Mine, and the Howth men will not go near it.

Why does it matter? Because Bri Leith is the realm's nearest neighbour among the mounds. The lord of the valley went in and shut his door and left his servants keeping it, and the realm lives in his front garden. The hermit says the mound's door will open again one day. He says it the way old men say it will rain.
legend: Valley of Bri Leith, east of Lough Derg, levels 10-50. Caille is the town in the valley floor (Ainrebh: Unnatural Powers; Lysagh's Problem; Brynn), Brynach a small stop north of it, and Druim Cain the frontier fort at the south end (teleport, trainers, siege merchant). The Coruscating Mine entrance is in the high western hills. Camps: barca, primroses, sheeries and veil wisps (10-17) near Caille, faerie horses and drakes (18-26) in the north meadow, siog siabra on the western hills (15-34), mad changelings (26-30) across Moon Lake, empyreans (34-44) on the eastern heights. Named: Mikka (50) by the Old Hermit's tent, Guardian Hru and Niy the Overseer (40), Riocard and his Albion druids up high in the west (Cad Goddeau D). The Old Hermit is the end of every Cad Goddeau step. Caille custom: never ride a horse from the faerie meadow, however tame it looks.

book.title: What the Hermit Remembers, written in his tent by the faerie meadow
pages: I am old and I sleep a great deal. When I wake the realm sends children to me with things in their hands, and I take the things and send the children away and go back to sleep. Between the sleeping and the waking I remember. This book is what I remember, for anyone who comes to the tent while I am asleep and wants to know why they were sent. I write it in pieces. The pieces do not always agree. That is the nature of a long memory, and of a short temper, which I also have.

I remember when the lord of the mound went in. The valley was his, all of it, and his servants were bright and many, and when the Veil came down he went into the hill and shut the door, and told his servants to keep it. They are keeping it still, up on the eastern heights. They have not had a word from him in longer than your realm has had a name, and they do not know that this is strange. Servants who have been told to wait do not ask how long.

I remember the song of the trees. It is older than me and older than the mound, and it makes trees stand up and fight, and the bards across the sea in the land of the Britons have a poem about it, badly remembered. A druid of theirs came over the water with five others and keeps a high place in the west of my valley and wants the song. I do not give it to him. The realm's children bring me his head now and then, and he grows another, and comes back.

I remember the valley before the siabra of the hills and the changelings across the lake. I remember the court cutting its door in the western hills into the mine. I remember a young map-reader camping beside me with half a map, and Howth's chief saying it led to a king's silver hand. That was not long ago. When the children come with their plant and their key and their jewel, I wake, and I remember all of it at once, and it is a great weight, and then I sleep again.
